input: Rate constants for a first-order liquid-phase reaction were measured at two temperatures. The rate constant $k$ was 0.084 s-1 at 300 K and 2.176 s-1 at 340 K. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4% at each temperature. The value at 340 K is a derived value, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1. The measured value at 300 K is the anchor for that computation: the Arrhenius relation carries $k$ from the measured temperature to the higher temperature at the stated activation energy. Between 300 K and 340 K, $k$ increases by a factor of 25.9 over an interval of 40 K, a steep temperature dependence for a liquid-phase reaction. The scatter of the triplicate measurements is small against that change: a relative standard deviation of 4% leaves the increase between the two temperatures far outside the range that measurement noise could produce. No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and samples drawn at higher temperatures no longer represented the reacting liquid, so measurements above that temperature were not used. The reported values therefore cover the full range in which sampling kept the liquid intact. Any rate constant quoted above 340 K for this system would rest on samples whose composition had already changed during collection. Within the measured range, the pair of values gives the temperature sensitivity of the reaction on a stated basis: one measured rate constant, one rate constant derived from it through the Arrhenius relation, and a precision of 4% attaching to the measurements at both temperatures. Sampling at each temperature followed the same procedure, so the two values are comparable on one basis, and the comparison between them does not mix two sampling methods.
